source.title: When Babies Teach Babies: Can student knowledge sharing outperform Teacher-Guided Distillation on small datasets?

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some table formatting is flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports performance for DWML students of different parameter counts, providing a different-measure test of the downstream-performance-with-scale part of V6. It does not test the original held-out-loss scaling measurement.
record.gate_note: The paper reports an average-accuracy comparison across four DWML model sizes, which bears on V6. It does not report held-out pretraining cross-entropy, power-law fits, extrapolation from smaller runs, or a compute-optimal allocation experiment. Chinchilla scaling findings mentioned in the introduction are background citations, not results of this study.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (co-trained BabyLM 10M students, 28M–60M), the paper reports downstream average accuracy by model size and calls it a positive size–performance correlation. This bears on V6 only; there are no loss sweeps, fits or allocation experiments.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that teacher-less methods can match or exceed teacher-supervised distillation, with simple Self-Distillation strongest and DWML giving modest gains over RoBERTa-base. They say performance correlated strongly with model size and learned peer weights, which they claim aligns with Chinchilla.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains and evaluates compact DWML students; it does not apply a scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation recipe.
record.problems: The scale comparison covers only four relatively small DWML models in one dataset setting. The reported average-accuracy aggregation is not further specified, and no uncertainty estimates are given. No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fit is reported.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss measured against parameters, tokens or compute.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation to larger runs.
No controlled comparison of shape at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime is analysed for power-law form.
No link between downstream scores and pretraining loss. No functional form or prediction is tested. Scale covers only about 2x (28M–60M).
No exponents or fitting choices are analysed.

missing.what: Per-benchmark scores by peer size for SD, KD, KD_DWML, DML and DWML. Several show the smallest (28M) peer scoring best, i.e. non-monotonic or reversed size effects.
Per-benchmark DWML 4-peer scores by size: BLiMP 50.0/50.5/50.0/50.5 and EWoK 50.0/49.8/49.1/50.3, which are non-monotonic.

record.verdict_notes: The size ablation compares four peers trained jointly with mutual KL distillation, with architectures chosen by Bayesian optimisation. Size is therefore confounded with shape and with peer interaction. All scores sit around 50%, close to chance on these minimal-pair tasks, and no uncertainty is reported. The Chinchilla mention is background only.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No fits on small runs or predictions for larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison of parameter and token allocations.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
No test of power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.

The reported comparison is limited to average accuracy across small DWML students trained on the BabyLM 10M dataset; it does not relate downstream scores to pretraining loss or establish predictability across tasks or orders of magnitude.
No analysis of scaling-law exponents, fit choices, or departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: 60M parameter model
rows.operation_detail: Compare DWML student models of different parameter counts.
rows.locator: Section 5.3, Effect of Model Size; Figure 2(c)
rows.note: The text reports this as the highest average accuracy among the four stated model sizes; the precise benchmark aggregation is not further specified.
rows.check: Baseline should be the 28M peer (49.63%). The gain is +1.26pp at near-chance accuracy with no uncertainty. Peers are co-trained with mutual KL, so sizes are not independent runs, and architecture (layers, heads, width) varies alongside size.

rows.subject: 42M parameter model
rows.operation_detail: Compare DWML student models of different parameter counts.
rows.locator: Section 5.3, Effect of Model Size; Figure 2(c)
rows.note: The text reports this as the second-highest average accuracy among the four stated model sizes; the precise benchmark aggregation is not further specified.
rows.check: Baseline should be the 28M peer. The gain is +0.5pp, near chance, with no uncertainty. Same co-training and architecture confound as R1.

rows.subject: 34M parameter model
rows.operation_detail: Compare DWML student models of different parameter counts.
rows.locator: Section 5.3, Effect of Model Size; Figure 2(c)
rows.note: The text reports this average accuracy for the 34M model; it is only 0.02 percentage points above the 28M model.
rows.check: Only 0.02pp above the 28M peer, which is no effect beyond noise. The 34M peer also differs sharply in shape (32 layers, hidden size 128).

rows.subject: 28M parameter model
rows.operation_detail: Compare DWML student models of different parameter counts.
rows.locator: Section 5.3, Effect of Model Size; Figure 2(c)
rows.note: The text reports this average accuracy for the smallest stated model size.
rows.check: This is the smallest model and serves as the reference point; it shows no scaling effect by itself. It should be recorded as the baseline for R1–R3 rather than as a result.

relationships.reason: Accuracy rises monotonically but only by about 1.3pp, near chance and without uncertainty. The 34M and 28M peers are essentially equal (R1–R4).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased monotonically by about 1.3 percentage points without reported uncertainty, with 28M and 34M peers essentially tied.

relationships.condition: SD and KD peers, and DWML on EWoK, BabyLM 10M
relationships.reason: Based on the text, since no rows exist: on BLiMP Supplement the 28M peer scores best for SD (56.53 vs 53.03 at 60M) and KD (55.82 vs 53.73). DWML EWoK is also best at 28M (50.3 vs 50.0).
relationships.display_finding: The 28M peer led BLiMP Supplement for SD, 56.53 versus 53.03 at 60M, and KD, 55.82 versus 53.73, and also led DWML EWoK, 50.3 versus 50.0.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: DWML students of 28M–60M parameters trained on BabyLM 10M
reader_labels.reason: Average accuracy rises across the reported sizes, but the 34M and 28M results are nearly identical and the small-size comparison does not establish a predictive scaling relationship; see R1–R4.
